newsitem.title: USA: US warns EU not to impede farm trade over biotech.
newsitem.headline: US warns EU not to impede farm trade over biotech.

text.p: U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky sternly warned European leaders Wednesday to expect a U.S. response if they allow domestic concerns over biotechnology to disrupt U.S. agricultural trade.

In testimony before the Senate Agriculture Committee, Barshefsky said the U.S. would not tolerate any reduction in its agricultural exports to the European Union stemming from an E.U proposal to require the segregation and labeling of genetically-modified food products.
Barshefsky estimated that the E.U. proposal for segregating and labelling could disrupt $4-5 billion in annual U.S. agricultural exports to the region.
The U.S., "at the minimum," would seek a World Trade Organization dispute settlement panel if the E.U. adopts such a requirement, Barshefsky said.
Speaking to reporters after the hearing, Barshefsky declined to say what other action the U.S. might take.

Both Barshefsky and U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman, who also testified on Wednesday before the panel, said they expressed U.S. concerns directly to E.U. Agriculture Commissioner Franz Fischler, who was here for talks Monday.
"We have taken a very strong stand on this" because of the large volume of trade at stake, Barshefsky said.

In response to European consumer concerns, Fischler has proposed a labeling system that would require genetically-modified soybeans, corn and other crops be kept separate throughout the marketing chain.
Sen. Tom Harkin, Iowa Democrat, noted during the hearing it would "be difficult and costly, if not impossible" to keep genetically-modified crops separate from traditional crops.
So far, there has been little U.S. public concern about genetically-modified crops, which U.S. farmers having been planting in greater numbers because of their higher yields.

But the issue "scares the heck out of European politicians," Glickman said, noting that the strong opposition of certain environmental groups has added to public skepticism over the safety of the crops.
